lessons.title: Getting to Know You
originalNarrativeRubric: Teacher-scored assessment rubric (0-2 each; total 8): 1) independently writes a statistical question anticipating variability; 2) identifies numerical versus categorical responses with a reason; 3) records and summarizes genuine or explicitly fictional responses without personal identifiers; 4) explains a justified interpretation and a sampling limitation. Award 0 for missing/incorrect, 1 for partially supported, 2 for specific and correct evidence. This task requires human review; no synthetic survey submission may be marked as a real participation grade.

structuredCriteria.evidence: independent question anticipates variation and is justified
distinguishes numerical, categorical, and non-statistical with reason
correctly documents true anonymized responses or explicitly fictional exercise; no invented participation
defensible summary, fourth-question category and sample/generalization limit

lessons.title: Data Representations
originalNarrativeRubric: Student tasks: (1) create a dot plot of all twelve measurements and identify its mode(s); (2) draw both histograms, specifying boundaries and labels, and explain how their appearances differ; (3) calculate the summary and draw the matching box plot; (4) compare what individual values a dot plot preserves versus what each grouped display hides. Teacher rubric: 0–2 points each for accurate dot counts, histograms and axis/interval labels, correct five-number calculation and box positions, and a reasoned graphical comparison. Maximum 8; 0 missing/incorrect, 1 partially correct, 2 complete and justified. Original drawing and reasoning require human review.

structuredCriteria.evidence: correct dot frequencies, value count and units
correct width 10 and width 5 nonoverlapping bins, total count, labels
min 46, Q1 58, median 66.5, Q3 76, max 92 and box geometry
explains what dot, histogram and box plots show/hide and limits from sample

lessons.title: A Gallery of Data
originalNarrativeRubric: Teacher-scored original gallery assessment rubric (0-2 each, total 8): accurate raw-data-to-display mapping, mathematically correct measures of center/spread, evidence-based comparison of two displays, and reasoned critique of labels/scale/limitations. A complete answer earns 2, partly supported 1, missing or wrong 0. The student-created displays and explanations are human-judged; do not treat a single numeric response as completing this lesson.

structuredCriteria.name: accurate original dot plots, histogram and box plot

lessons.title: The Shape of Distributions
originalNarrativeRubric: Teacher-scored rubric: give 0, 1 or 2 points each for accurate classification, numerical justification, plausible context with variable and units, and reasoned critique of partner claims (8 maximum). This is an explanation/card-matching activity, not a single machine-graded number. The first-party frequency tables are not publisher artwork.

V12 activity fidelity: the publisher explicitly includes a Which One Does Not Belong discussion and partner matching of ten representations, followed by suggesting a plausible real-world context for a displayed distribution. Students must invent at least two plausible contexts for one of the fictional graphs and explain why the source data cannot be inferred uniquely from a shape. The plotted dot positions and frequency cards must be student-created, not auto-inferred from rubric text.

lessons.title: Calculating Measures of Center and Variability
originalNarrativeRubric: Teacher-scored rubric: 0–2 each for sorted data and stated quartile rule, correct mean/median, all absolute deviations and MAD, and comparison with appropriate units (8 maximum). Teacher judgement is required for explanation and interpretation; a numeric answer cannot stand in for a physical meter-stick investigation.

V12 proposed teacher rubric (0–2 each, total8): original seven-point data plot and quartiles; correct mean, median, IQR and MAD with units; explanation and chosen quartile convention; genuine activity/diagnostic evidence if performed. Optional status must be respected in reporting.

lessons.title: Mystery Computations
originalNarrativeRubric: Teacher-scored rubric: 0–2 each for entering or describing a valid formula, using at least three contrasting trials, explaining the inferred relationship, and checking a counterexample (8 total). Unobserved clicking or partner discussion must never receive synthetic automatic credit.

structuredCriteria.name: live cell-reference formula validated with three trials
partner rule discovery without fabricated technology evidence

lessons.title: Spreadsheet Computations
originalNarrativeRubric: Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, total 8): correct formula syntax, defensible estimate and units, verified arithmetic, and authentic or explicitly simulated recalculation explanation. A correct number alone does not verify that spreadsheet work occurred.

structuredCriteria.evidence: accurate change-propagation explanation, labelled simulated if not run
units/constraints, justified counterexample or independent check

lessons.title: Spreadsheet Shortcuts
originalNarrativeRubric: Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, maximum 8): correct relative reference and copy behavior, all expected values, valid recurrence and direct expression, and correct inequality boundary with honest evidence about the interaction. No simulated clicking or dragging can be claimed as observed usage.

structuredCriteria.evidence: accurate change-propagation explanation, labelled simulated if not run
units/constraints, justified counterexample or independent check

lessons.title: Technological Graphing
originalNarrativeRubric: Student tasks: supply a screenshot or accessible text table of the data and numerical results, recreate the three displays using authorized statistical technology or a clearly labelled paper simulation, change a single value and histogram class width, and critique any misleading interpretation. Real data from a prior anonymous survey can replace invented data only when actually available. Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, max 8): correctly entered data and formulas; correct calculated statistics; correctly labeled and compared displays; reasoned changed-value/bin-width interpretation. Do not assert software interaction without observed evidence.

lessons.title: The Effect of Extremes
originalNarrativeRubric: Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, maximum 8): correct raw-data/changed-data statistics; accurate shape/tail analysis; valid constrained example with independent mean/median checks; defensible choice of center and ethical treatment of outliers. No invented classroom response or fabricated software action counts as evidence.

lessons.title: Comparing and Contrasting Data Distributions
originalNarrativeRubric: Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 each for accurate displays, correct two MADs, correct two IQRs and a comparative argument linking display shape and spread (maximum 8). Different correct graphs or explanations require human interpretation.

lessons.title: Standard Deviation
originalNarrativeRubric: Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 for correct mean, squared-deviation table and division by n, correct square root with units, meaningful A/B comparison and honest software-check evidence (max 8). A single numeric result does not prove software use or contextual understanding.

lessons.title: More Standard Deviation
originalNarrativeRubric: Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 each for asking relevant missing information, correct mean/SD and units, meaningful comparison acknowledging limitations, and independently justified shift-invariance claim (8 max). This info-gap reasoning and dialogue are human assessed.

lessons.title: Outliers
originalNarrativeRubric: Student activity: reproduce the box plot, show both 1.5-IQR fences, compare mean and median with/without the suspected outlier, propose a verification procedure, and write a justified reporting recommendation. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 for accurate quartiles/fences, correct changes in center, defensible source investigation, and transparent reporting (max 8).

lessons.title: Comparing Data Sets
originalNarrativeRubric: Teacher-scored rubric: 0–2 points each for accurate means/medians, accurate IQR/SD, a comparison using common axes and units, and a defensible choice with stated goal and critique (maximum 8). Player-selection reasoning is human reviewed, not automatically graded as one fixed preference.

lessons.title: Analyzing Data
originalNarrativeRubric: Teacher-scored rubric, 0–2 each (maximum 8): safe and comparable experimental design; correctly documented genuine observations or transparent simulation limitation; accurate displays/statistics; evidence-backed conclusion identifying confounding, measurement error and sampling limitations. Do not fabricate participants, trial counts, saved answers or physical evidence.

lessons.title: Planning a Pizza Party
originalNarrativeRubric: Teacher rubric, 0–2 each (8 maximum): correct variable definitions with integer/nonnegative domains, valid expression/equation and at least two inequalities, independently checked feasible plan with units, and justified assumptions with alternative/critique. Never claim an original student party plan or actual restaurant quote was collected if it was not.

lessons.title: Writing Equations to Model Relationships (Part 1)
originalNarrativeRubric: Student activity: interpret equations from words and vice versa, write at least one additive equation, multiplicative cost equation, percentage model and simple geometric relationship, state all units and domains, and peer-review a model for whether its assumptions are justified. Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, 8 maximum): correct constant/variable meanings, faithful equation construction, mathematical and domain accuracy, and reasoned critique and contextual interpretation.

Teacher human rubric 0–2 each for exact percentage calculations, correct polyhedral relationship and limits, clear fixed versus variable quantities/units, and a defensible tax/constraint equation with independent reasoning.

structuredCriteria.name: Tax constraint and peer assumption critique

lessons.title: Writing Equations to Model Relationships (Part 2)
originalNarrativeRubric: Student activity: work from an unknown table, propose and reject candidate equations, extend it to an unlisted input, construct a matching word problem, and critique a partner's table or graph for units and restrictions. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 points each for table differences/products, correct equation and domain, checked predictions, and valid contextual explanation (maximum 8). Avoid auto-grading a unique formula as the only possible mathematical description of finitely many points.

structuredCriteria.name: four correctly matched table rules and units
inverse area and prize model with domain

lessons.title: Equations and Their Solutions
originalNarrativeRubric: Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, total 8): interprets one-variable solution, verifies one true and one false candidate with substitution, interprets an ordered pair and domain, and gives a coherent contextual explanation. A multiple-choice check alone does not replace the source reasoning.

lessons.title: Equations and Their Graphs
originalNarrativeRubric: Student task: sketch or graph electronically the line and the feasible whole-number model, test candidate points, exchange a context with a peer and explain what an off-graph point would claim. Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, max 8): correctly labelled graph, correct substitution checks, context and domain explanation, correct technology disclosure (real graphing versus manual drawing).

lessons.title: Equivalent Equations
originalNarrativeRubric: Student tasks: explain each transformation to a partner, generate two distinct equivalent forms of a contextual equation, test plausible wrong and correct moves, then interpret both equations in words. Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, total 8): exact solution-set comparison, valid move justification, correct contextual variable relation, and critique of a non-equivalent transformation.

lessons.title: Explaining Steps for Rewriting Equations
originalNarrativeRubric: Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, 8 max): correct original solution sets; explanation of valid moves; demonstration of division-by-variable pitfall; accurate no-solution and undefined-expression reasoning. It is not enough to record a final numeric value.

lessons.title: Which Variable to Solve for? (Part 1)
originalNarrativeRubric: Student task: read equations, identify which variable a question asks for, isolate it using reversible moves and substitute at least two valid inputs. Include a sensible unit and domain for every variable. Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, max 8): correct target, valid isolation, correct verification with units and coherent contextual explanation. One formula alone does not establish modeling understanding.

lessons.title: Which Variable to Solve for? (Part 2)
originalNarrativeRubric: Student task: rearrange the equation in two ways (solve c in terms of t, t in terms of c), build a labelled table, test boundaries including negative and non-integer outputs, and critique a partner's feasible cargo plan. Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, 8 maximum): correct transformation, valid domain, correct boundary and rounding, and explanation of technology simulation versus observed tool use.

lessons.title: Connecting Equations to Graphs (Part 1)
originalNarrativeRubric: Student activity: build original graphs of 2x+5y=30 and x+4y=20 with consistent scales; interpret each intercept and negative slope; defend which points meet real-world restrictions and why points off the line do not spend exactly the budget. Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, 8 maximum): correct intercepts, correctly labelled graph, domain/rate interpretation, and valid solution classification with an explicit reason. The physical graph and reasoning are teacher reviewed.

lessons.title: Connecting Equations to Graphs (Part 2)
originalNarrativeRubric: Student task: graph two independently authored lines, rewrite their equations without changing the solution sets, test two points per line and explain an off-graph pair. Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, max 8): valid isolation, numerical slope/intercepts, graph/scale, and contextual explanation with verified substitution.

lessons.title: Writing and Graphing Systems of Linear Equations
originalNarrativeRubric: Student task: draw both independent original lines, mark the meaningful first-quadrant integer intersection, identify two other pairs that satisfy only one constraint, and explain why a correct system requires all restrictions. Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, max 8): appropriate variable definitions, accurate graphs and shared scale, verified intersection, and interpretation of why off-intersection pairs fail.

lessons.title: Solving Systems by Substitution
originalNarrativeRubric: Student task: work one system by two substitution pathways, annotate which expression is replacing which variable, and check each final pair with the original constraints. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 each for correct substitution, equation-solving steps, back-substitution checks and explanatory method choice.

lessons.title: Solving Systems by Elimination (Part 1)
originalNarrativeRubric: Student task: make an original visual balance diagram or equivalent text table, add/subtract two equations, graph both originals and their sum, describe the single shared intersection and justify why it survives the operation. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 for correct operation, cancellation, back-substitution and graph/argument; group-created diagrams are not single-number auto-grades.

lessons.title: Solving Systems by Elimination (Part 2)
originalNarrativeRubric: Partner task: write and justify an addition proof and a subtraction proof; critique a calculation where only left sides were combined, and verify solutions with arithmetic and a shared coordinate graph. Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, 8 max): correct elimination, justification of equal additions, verified pair, and contextual/graph interpretation.

lessons.title: Solving Systems by Elimination (Part 3)
originalNarrativeRubric: Student task: choose a multiplier rather than copy an unexamined recipe, solve both systems, explain why multiplying by zero would be invalid, and check the resulting ordered pairs. Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, 8 max): suitable multiplier, correct elimination, proper full-system verification, and logical justification that all solutions were preserved.

lessons.title: Systems of Linear Equations and Their Solutions
originalNarrativeRubric: Student task: graph the three systems, classify and justify each solution cardinality by both algebra and visual features, provide one valid pair for the infinite system, and critique any wrong classification. Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, max 8): correct classifications, tested solution pairs, correct slope/intercept reasoning and coherent graphical explanation.

lessons.title: Representing Situations with Inequalities
originalNarrativeRubric: Student task: invent two plausible workshop modifications, represent each with multiple inequalities and test boundary cases that distinguish strict and inclusive limits. Partner critique should catch missing units and missing integer restrictions. Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, max 8): variable meaning, correctly translated comparison, valid combined feasible set and boundary/context explanation.

lessons.title: Solutions to Inequalities in One Variable
originalNarrativeRubric: Student task: derive both inequality ranges, show at least three substitution trials around each boundary, draw two labeled number lines, interpret integer restrictions for students and critique whether equality should be allowed. Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, max 8): variable and inequality model, correct open/closed boundary, positive/negative and integer tests, contextual explanation and critique.

lessons.title: Writing and Solving Inequalities in One Variable
originalNarrativeRubric: Student task: solve dinner constraint, check x=10.4 versus x=10.5, explain whether food can be fractionally purchased, and classify structural inequalities with zero, negative and positive values. Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, 8 max): correct translation, algebra and inequality direction, boundary/domain interpretation, and reasoned structural checks.

lessons.title: Graphing Linear Inequalities in Two Variables (Part 1)
originalNarrativeRubric: Student task: independently create the line and plot at least four solutions and four non-solutions, distinguish the solid/dashed boundary, and exchange explanations. Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, max 8): correct boundary and intercepts, accurate point classification, correct shading and inequality symbol, and justified graphic interpretation with accessible text.

lessons.title: Graphing Linear Inequalities in Two Variables (Part 2)
originalNarrativeRubric: Student task: manually sketch and label the feasible first-quadrant region, classify boundary/off-boundary points, suggest a landscape allocation that uses less than full funds and another that uses exactly full funds, then critique peer claims about negative areas. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 each for correct model, accurate region, truthful point checks and justified contextual feasibility.

lessons.title: Solving Problems with Inequalities in Two Variables
originalNarrativeRubric: Student activity: match at least two independently made graph windows, an inequality, a verbal budget interpretation and a candidate point; use graphing technology to verify region and line inclusion where actually available. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 each for correct model, boundaries and shading, point/classification checks, and authentic or explicitly simulated graphing explanation.

lessons.title: Solutions to Systems of Linear Inequalities in Two Variables
originalNarrativeRubric: Student task: graph each original half-plane and the overlapping solution region, distinguish points meeting only one condition from points meeting both, then defend a candidate fabric allocation. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 each for equations and domains, correctly shaded overlap, exact point tests, and justified interpretation including boundary inclusion.

lessons.title: Solving Problems with Systems of Linear Inequalities in Two Variables
originalNarrativeRubric: Student task: create one graph for inclusive system and another after a strict change, label feasible points, explain the status of (20,0) and a non-integer point and propose an additional relevant resource constraint. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 each for complete system, boundary status, numerical testing and explanatory graph/assumption critique.

lessons.title: Modeling with Systems of Inequalities in Two Variables
originalNarrativeRubric: Student task: propose a different two-ingredient original model with at least three inequalities/equalities, find and explain its feasible region, check one boundary point and one invalid point and critique the sensitivity to changed per-unit parameters. Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, total 8): meaningful variables and source assumptions, accurate constraints/domains, calculated feasible region, and evidence-backed model evaluation and limitations. Never pretend to have prepared or tasted trail mix.

lessons.title: Two-way Tables
originalNarrativeRubric: Student task: reconstruct a partially hidden table by asking a partner which row and column totals are known, calculate missing cells, interpret counts in words, and justify how totals expose a miscopied entry. Do not claim responses came from actual classmates. Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, 8 max): correctly structured and labelled table, accurate internal/marginal/grand totals, clear interpretation and reasoned information-gap questions.

originalNarrativeRubric: Student task: construct three separately titled relative-frequency tables using the overall sample, row and column denominators, calculate complements, and explain why 30%, 60% and 57.14% can all describe the same interior cell without disagreement. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 for denominator selection, correct row/column calculations, labelled percentages and justified comparison and critique.

lessons.title: Associations in Categorical Data
originalNarrativeRubric: Student task: create a labelled pair of side-by-side bar representations and compare row percentages, design a 'no association' table and critique a claim of causation. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 each for accurate conditional frequencies, valid comparison, appropriate no-association example and careful association-versus-causation language.

lessons.title: Linear Models
originalNarrativeRubric: Student task: plot the four points and a defensible line manually or with actually observed technology, choose a competing line, justify which fits better, interpret slope/intercept and critique an extrapolated claim. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 each for plot, plausible fit and residuals, correct rate/initial-value meaning and limits of prediction.

lessons.title: Fitting Lines
originalNarrativeRubric: Student task: rank two lines by residual totals, use actual software if available to confirm least-squares coefficients, critique an outlier's effect and explain that line choice is based on an objective such as squared-error minimum. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 each for correct fit arithmetic, two compared residual series, interpretation of model and actual or transparently simulated technology use.

lessons.title: Residuals
originalNarrativeRubric: Teacher-scored rubric: 0–2 each for correct predicted values, signed residuals and zero-axis plot, reasoned pattern-based model critique, and appropriate contextual/technology limits (maximum 8). An automatically graded residual number alone does not demonstrate the source plotting and critique tasks.

lessons.title: The Correlation Coefficient
originalNarrativeRubric: Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, maximum 8): accurate direction/strength assignment, evidence from point trends, correct handling of nonlinear/undefined cases, and critical interpretation with no causal overclaim. Human reasoning and actual plotted evidence matter.

lessons.title: Using the Correlation Coefficient
originalNarrativeRubric: Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 each for correctly entered paired-data evidence or disclosed hand calculation, independently justified r computation, direction/strength interpretation, and critical discussion of nonlinearity, outliers and causation. An authored table or a calculator-looking number does not prove actual device use.

lessons.title: Causal Relationships
originalNarrativeRubric: Student activity: describe two distinct causal hypotheses and a confounding variable for a bivariate association, draw a simple accessible arrows-and-variables diagram, design a feasible ethical follow-up analysis, and critique a headline claiming cause from correlation. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 for appropriate statistical observation, candidate explanations, study-design limitations and responsible causal-language critique.

lessons.title: Fossils and Flags
originalNarrativeRubric: Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 each (maximum 8): valid research question and source/provenance; transparent genuine observations or simulated limitation; accurate scatter/line/residual/correlation analysis with units; and defensible interpretation identifying selection bias and avoiding causal overclaims. Never grant synthetic fieldwork credit.

lessons.title: Describing and Graphing Situations
originalNarrativeRubric: Student task: sketch the toy motion graph and independently label rates, classify three different tables as functions or nonfunctions, construct a counterexample relation and explain why it fails. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 each for input/output definition, valid classification with evidence, correctly labelled motion graph and reasoned verbal critique (8 maximum). Do not claim a publisher photograph or actual physical motion was reproduced.

lessons.title: Function Notation
originalNarrativeRubric: Student task: interpret at least five original notations with explicit units, map them to a labelled graph and table, explain why H(2) is different from 2H, and translate contextual data to notation in both directions. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 each for correctly named function and argument, accurate units, correct graph/table match and verbal interpretation.

lessons.title: Interpreting & Using Function Notation
originalNarrativeRubric: Student task: describe values on three labeled time intervals, sketch the original piecewise function from statements, compare at least four input-output pairs, and explain what inequalities imply about the graph. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 each for input/output interpretation, correct comparisons, coherent drawn graph and domain/time-interval reasoning.

comparison with same named function and different contexts

lessons.title: Using Function Notation to Describe Rules (Part 1)
originalNarrativeRubric: Student task: write generalized symbolic rules from two different verbal instructions, evaluate a table of input-output pairs and solve one equation from a known function output, checking domains. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 for correct function rule, correct evaluation and reverse-solving, contextual/domain interpretation and explanation of equivalence between tables and equations.

lessons.title: Using Function Notation to Describe Rules (Part 2)
originalNarrativeRubric: Student task: generate both graphs and compare their rates, solve two target-output equations by algebra and graph reading, and document whether real graphing technology was used or drawings were manual. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 each for accurate evaluation, inverse input-solving, mathematical evidence of linearity/nonlinearity and correct labelled graphs plus technology disclosure.

lessons.title: Features of Graphs
originalNarrativeRubric: Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, maximum 8): faithful graph with axes/units, correct intercepts/extrema, correct interval analysis, and meaningful function-notation/context explanations. Actual graph creation and open reasoning are teacher assessed; no invented student activity is automatically credited.

lessons.title: Using Graphs to Find Average Rate of Change
originalNarrativeRubric: Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 each for correct endpoint readings, signed Δoutput/Δinput arithmetic, units and direction interpretation, and critical rate comparison with limitations. A graph read from a teacher/student source is not reproduced as publisher artwork.

lessons.title: Interpreting and Creating Graphs
originalNarrativeRubric: Student activity: draw two different plausible graphs from an underspecified situation, label intercepts/maxima/constant intervals and explain their common and different features. State that actual publisher video clips are not supplied in this first-party JSON; do not imply a video was watched or produced. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 each for faithful context model, accurate graph/features and rates, explicit assumptions, and critique of an alternative valid graph.

lessons.title: Comparing Graphs
originalNarrativeRubric: Student activity: graph both lines on common time/balance axes, label their intersection and relative position before/after, translate symbolic comparisons into everyday language, and consider how to change deposit amounts to move the crossing. Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, max 8): accurate shared-axis graph, checked comparisons and intersection, correct rate/intercept interpretation, and justified contextual explanation.

lessons.title: Domain and Range (Part 1)
originalNarrativeRubric: Student task: sort proposed inputs and outputs for both functions, explain why 8.5 participants and negative lengths are impossible, state domain/range in lists or inequalities as appropriate, and critique an unsupported continuous graph in a discrete situation. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 for correct variable/domain, correctly enumerated range, graph/context distinction and reasoning about boundary cases.

lessons.title: Domain and Range (Part 2)
originalNarrativeRubric: Student task: draw both graphs with accurate open/closed points; decide whether a graph includes certain inputs and outputs; compare two graphs with identical x-domain but different ranges; and explain why a jump in graph excludes intermediate output values. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 for endpoints, domain, range and coherent context explanation with suitable accessible alternatives.

lessons.title: Piecewise Functions
originalNarrativeRubric: Student task: construct a table including 0,4.9,5,5.01,8,8.1; draw the curve/step with labelled axes, contrast an incorrectly closed second-branch left endpoint with the correct graph, and create a second real-life step-fee function. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 each for correct cases notation, boundary tests, accurate graph and clear context/domain explanation.

lessons.title: Absolute Value Functions (Part 1)
originalNarrativeRubric: Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 each: accurate genuine or explicitly hypothetical data provenance, correct absolute-error calculation, clear graph with labelled axes and vertex, and defensible rule/generalization with noted limitation (8 max). Do not grant physical observation credit from a fabricated dataset.

lessons.title: Absolute Value Functions (Part 2)
originalNarrativeRubric: Student activity: sketch f(x), d(x), g(x) with common axes, compare vertex/range, convert at least one to cases and critique a wrong transformation claim. Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, total 8): accurate distance interpretation, correct cases and endpoint, accurate graph/vertex, and clear explanations of translations.

lessons.title: Inverse Functions
originalNarrativeRubric: Student activity: invent a three-letter cipher message, encode and exchange with a partner, explain why the decoding must undo the steps in reverse, then compare it with numerical conversion. lessons.title: Finding and Interpreting Inverse Functions
